# Visualization {#sec-visualization}

Visualization serves three related analytical purposes: to discover patterns
in data, to diagnose the adequacy of a proposed explanation, and to
communicate a result to a specified audience. The analysis in @sec-eda
used graphics for exploration; the present chapter examines how choices
about aggregation, visual encoding, and annotation determine which comparisons a
reader can make. A figure is therefore a sequence of analytical decisions
rather than a decorative rendering of a completed calculation. The analyst
selects eligible records, defines the quantity of interest, maps that
quantity to visible marks, and supplies enough context to evaluate the
result. Each decision can change the apparent pattern even when the source
data remain fixed. The same principles will apply to prediction and
diagnostic figures in @sec-modeling. The worked examples use NYPD-directed 311
illegal-parking requests created during September 6–12, 2026; maps and a
small simulated dataset expose design problems that the request records
alone cannot isolate [@munzner2014visualization; @wilke2019fundamentals].

The goal of this chapter is to provide a procedure that can be applied when
the appropriate figure is not specified in advance. The procedure begins
with a substantive question and a definition of the observational unit,
eligible records, measurement, and comparison. It then requires a visual
form that preserves the information needed for that comparison, followed by
a review of the inference a reader is likely to draw. The code examples
make these decisions visible, while the exercises progressively transfer
responsibility for the question, chart form, and data source to students
preparing a midterm project. A successful project figure must therefore be
accompanied by a defensible interpretation and a statement of its limits;
executable code alone does not establish that the graphic answers its
question. Earlier course demonstrations by Sonia Lucey (Plotnine),
Alejandro Haerter (GeoPandas), and Jack Perkins (Google Maps) informed the
selection of tools. The figures here use the current book data and can be
reproduced from the files distributed with this repository.

## Purpose

The purpose of a figure determines the data transformation and visual
encoding that are appropriate. A comparison of two numerical levels benefits
from positions on a common scale, because readers can judge aligned
positions more accurately than similar areas or color intensities
[@cleveland1984graphical; @mackinlay1986automating]. A question about a
distribution instead requires information about spread, shape, or tails;
two groups with equal means can have different distributions. A geographic
question may require points when individual recorded locations matter, or
polygons when the quantity has been aggregated to areas. These requirements
do not define a single universal chart type. Exploration may require
several displays that reveal different aspects of a dataset, whereas a
communication figure should make its principal comparison immediately
identifiable and still disclose the context that qualifies it. In either
case, the analyst must first specify the observational unit, measured
variable, eligible population, and observation period introduced in
@sec-problem-formulation and @sec-wrangling [@tussey2025principles]. A
change in any of these four elements changes the quantity the figure
represents.

The worked figures use the same screened request table as @sec-eda, but
they serve different reader tasks. The problem formulation in
@sec-problem-formulation established the request as the observational unit
and limited the interpretation of closure time; @sec-wrangling documented
the transformations; and @sec-eda examined
the resulting distributions. This chapter asks how a visual specification
can preserve those distinctions while making an intended comparison clear.
An hourly line plot summarizes all eligible requests, a closure-time
interval plot shows selected distributional features, and a point map
requires usable coordinates. The corresponding displays therefore do not
all contain the same records or support the same claim. The following code
loads the common screened table through its
[shared preparation function](scripts/parking_requests.py), derives only
the time fields needed for the examples, and reports counts that will
matter when the eligible set changes. This compact audit links each later
figure to a reproducible input without repeating the source import and
filtering procedure [@nycopendatand311].

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import (
    aes, facet_grid, facet_wrap, geom_line, geom_point, ggplot, labs,
    scale_color_manual, scale_x_continuous, theme, theme_minimal,
)
from scripts.parking_requests import load_parking_requests, load_zcta_context

parking = load_parking_requests()
parking["hour"] = parking["created_at"].dt.hour
parking["day_type"] = np.where(
    parking["created_at"].dt.dayofweek >= 5, "Weekend", "Weekday"
)

pd.Series({
    "requests": len(parking),
    "unique request IDs": parking["request_id"].nunique(),
    "missing coordinates": parking[["latitude", "longitude"]]
        .isna().any(axis=1).sum(),
}).to_frame("count")
```

The compact report establishes the denominator for the chapter's figures
and identifies the requests that cannot appear as points. The hourly and
closure-time displays use the full screened table, whereas a point map
must exclude rows without usable coordinates. The subset represented by
the map could differ systematically if missing locations are concentrated
in a borough or problem-detail group; marker transparency does not correct
that coverage difference. An area map introduces another eligibility rule
when it requires a five-digit ZIP label or a polygon assignment. Each
caption should therefore name its eligible records, measured quantity,
units, observation period, and any exclusion relevant to interpretation.
These facts belong next to the display because the same source archive can
produce different plotted populations. The locally held archive and its
provenance are documented in @sec-problem-formulation; the remaining
sections concentrate on how analysis choices become visible in a figure.

## Grammar of Graphics

The grammar of graphics provides a language for specifying how data become
a figure. Its components describe the choices that connect observations to
visible marks:

- **Data.** The data component identifies the observations and variables
  used by a layer.
- **Aesthetic mappings.** A mapping assigns variables to visual properties
  such as horizontal position, vertical position, color, or size; a fixed
  property is set independently of a variable.
- **Geometric marks.** A geom determines the marks used to display the data,
  such as points, lines, or bars.
- **Statistical transformations.** A statistical transformation summarizes
  or otherwise transforms observations before the geom draws them.
- **Scales.** A scale translates data values into visual values, such as
  positions on an axis or colors in a legend.
- **Coordinates.** A coordinate system specifies how mapped positions are
  arranged in the display, including the spatial frame used by a map.
- **Facets.** Facets repeat a common specification across subsets of the
  data so that panels can be compared.

This decomposition makes a figure revisable: an analyst can change a
mapping, geom, or facet layout without reconstructing the entire graphic.
Wilkinson developed the general framework, Wickham formalized a layered
implementation in ggplot2, and Plotnine implements that approach in Python
[@wilkinson2005grammar; @wickham2010layered; @plotnine2026facets].

The first grammar example compares the hours at which requests were
created on weekdays and weekend days. This observation week contains five
weekdays and two weekend days, so raw totals would give the weekday group
more exposure time. For borough $b$, day type $d$, and hour $h$, let
$n_{bdh}$ denote the number of requests and let $D_d$ denote the number of
observed days of type $d$. The plotted value is $n_{bdh}/D_d$, measured in
requests per observed day during hour $h$. The code first counts requests
for each combination, then inserts zeroes for combinations with no request,
and finally divides by $D_d$. Explicit zeroes are necessary because an
absent combination should appear at zero rather than disappear from a line.
This normalization addresses unequal numbers of observed weekdays and
weekend days. It does not adjust for borough population, the number of
vehicles, reporting propensity, or the possibility that a particular day
was unusual.

```{python}
borough_order = ["BRONX", "BROOKLYN", "MANHATTAN", "QUEENS", "STATEN ISLAND"]
hour_index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
    [borough_order, ["Weekday", "Weekend"], range(24)],
    names=["borough", "day_type", "hour"],
)
hourly = (
    parking.groupby(["borough", "day_type", "hour"])
    .size()
    .reindex(hour_index, fill_value=0)
    .rename("requests")
    .reset_index()
)
hourly["days_observed"] = hourly["day_type"].map(
    {"Weekday": 5, "Weekend": 2}
)
hourly["requests_per_day"] = hourly["requests"] / hourly["days_observed"]
hourly["borough"] = pd.Categorical(
    hourly["borough"], categories=borough_order, ordered=True
)
```

The Brooklyn figure demonstrates how a layered specification assigns a
different role to each visual component. Hour is mapped to horizontal
position, the normalized request count to vertical position, and day type
to color. The line geom connects adjacent hourly summaries within each day
type, while the point geom marks the 24 discrete hours from which those
lines are constructed. A connecting line helps readers follow the temporal
pattern, but it does not imply that requests were observed continuously
between the hourly bins. The manual color scale assigns stable colors to
the two categories, and the labeled horizontal breaks make the time scale
legible without printing every hour. The code supplies a legend because
color is mapped to a variable; changing a constant line color would not
create a second group. Brooklyn provides a compact example before the
same specification is repeated across boroughs. Readers should compare
the timing and level of recorded requests, while retaining the one-week
scope of the data [@heer2010crowdsourcing].

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-grammar
#| fig-cap: "Average requests per observed day by hour and day type in Brooklyn, September 6–12, 2026."
#| fig-alt: "Two lines compare the hourly pattern of Brooklyn illegal-parking requests on weekdays and weekend days."
#| fig-format: svg
brooklyn_hours = hourly.loc[hourly["borough"].eq("BROOKLYN")]
hour_plot = (
    ggplot(brooklyn_hours, aes("hour", "requests_per_day", color="day_type"))
    + geom_line(size=1)
    + geom_point(size=1.5)
    + scale_color_manual(values={"Weekday": "#3366AA", "Weekend": "#CC6677"})
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=[0, 6, 12, 18, 23])
    + labs(
        x="Hour request was created", y="Requests per observed day",
        color="Day type", title="When Brooklyn requests were created",
    )
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(figure_size=(7, 4))
)
hour_plot
```

Faceting extends the same grammar by repeating a common display for defined
subsets. In `facet_wrap()`, borough determines the panel, while color still
distinguishes day type within each panel. This arrangement helps a reader
compare the two temporal profiles in each borough and then scan for
differences across the city. In `facet_grid()`, day type determines rows
and borough determines columns. The resulting layout makes the two
grouping variables explicit in position, so color is no longer required
to identify day type. Both examples retain fixed vertical scales. Under
a fixed scale, a height in the Bronx has the same numerical meaning as
the same height in Brooklyn; the cost is that variation in a low-count
panel may be visually compressed. Free vertical scales emphasize shape
within panels but remove direct height comparability. The analyst should
choose between these alternatives according to whether the question
concerns absolute level or within-group temporal structure, and should
make that choice visible in the caption [@plotnine2026facets].

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-facet-wrap
#| fig-cap: "Average hourly request counts per observed day, with a separate panel for each borough."
#| fig-alt: "Five borough panels show weekday and weekend hourly request patterns with a common vertical scale."
#| fig-format: svg
(
    ggplot(hourly, aes("hour", "requests_per_day", color="day_type"))
    + geom_line(size=.8)
    + facet_wrap("borough", ncol=3)
    + scale_color_manual(values={"Weekday": "#3366AA", "Weekend": "#CC6677"})
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=[0, 6, 12, 18, 23])
    + labs(x="Hour request was created", y="Requests per observed day",
           color="Day type")
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(figure_size=(10, 6))
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-facet-grid
#| fig-cap: "The same hourly summaries arranged by day type (rows) and borough (columns), with fixed scales."
#| fig-alt: "A two-by-five grid compares hourly request patterns across weekday and weekend rows and borough columns."
#| fig-format: svg
(
    ggplot(hourly, aes("hour", "requests_per_day"))
    + geom_line(color="#3366AA", size=.8)
    + facet_grid("day_type ~ borough")
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=[0, 12, 23])
    + labs(x="Hour request was created", y="Requests per observed day")
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(figure_size=(12, 5))
)
```

The two facet arrangements answer related but distinct questions. The wrap
retains the colored weekday and weekend profiles in each borough, which
supports a within-borough comparison of their timing. The grid places
weekday and weekend profiles in separate rows, which reduces overlap but
requires readers to compare positions across panels. Neither layout
resolves a limitation in the underlying classification: Labor Day fell on
the Monday labeled as a weekday in this extract. The weekday average is
therefore an average over five calendar weekdays, one of which was a
holiday, rather than an estimate of a typical workday profile. If the
project question concerns ordinary commuting days, the analyst should
define a holiday indicator, obtain more weeks, or narrow the interpretation.
This example shows why visual grammar and study design must be considered
together. A technically correct facet specification can still organize
observations into groups that do not correspond to the intended substantive
comparison.

## Comparisons

A statistical figure should retain the aspect of the observations that is
needed to answer its question. Counts have a defined zero and can be
shown by lengths that begin at that reference; estimates or group summaries
often benefit from dots on a common axis, especially when several values
are close. Questions about spread, skewness, or unusual observations
require a distribution display or a summary that explicitly represents
variation. A mean bar cannot distinguish a tightly concentrated group
from a group with long tails [@cleveland1984graphical;
@weissgerber2015beyond]. The analyst must also distinguish comparisons of
levels from comparisons of change: a line is useful for an ordered sequence
such as time, but connecting unordered categories can imply an artificial
continuity. Color hue can identify categories, while ordered lightness can
represent magnitude. When color carries an essential distinction, position,
labels, or another redundant cue can help readers who cannot distinguish
the chosen hues [@crameri2020misuse; @harrower2003colorbrewer].

The closure-time example compares the three problem details with the most
requests in the selected week, so the selection rule precedes the display.
For each group, the code calculates the first quartile, median, and third
quartile of recorded closure hours. A dot locates the median on a shared
horizontal scale, and a line extends from the first to the third quartile.
That line describes the middle half of the observed closure times; it is
**not a confidence interval** for a population median or for the difference
between groups. A confidence interval would require an inferential target
and a procedure for quantifying sampling uncertainty, whereas these
quartiles summarize variation among records in the extract
[@correll2014error]. The figure complements the empirical cumulative
distribution in @sec-eda by making a small number of center-and-spread
comparisons easy to read. It does not replace the distribution display
when the shape or extreme tail of closure time is the main concern.

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-detail-intervals
#| fig-cap: "Median and middle-half range of recorded closure times for the three most reported illegal-parking details, September 6–12, 2026."
#| fig-alt: "Three horizontal point-and-interval marks compare median closure hours and the observed interquartile range."
#| fig-format: svg
top_details = parking["problem_detail"].value_counts().head(3).index
top = parking.loc[parking["problem_detail"].isin(top_details)]
detail_summary = (
    top.groupby("problem_detail")["closure_hours"]
    .quantile([.25, .5, .75])
    .unstack()
    .rename(columns={.25: "q25", .5: "median", .75: "q75"})
    .sort_values("median")
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
positions = range(len(detail_summary))
ax.errorbar(
    detail_summary["median"], positions,
    xerr=[detail_summary["median"] - detail_summary["q25"],
          detail_summary["q75"] - detail_summary["median"]],
    fmt="o", color="#3366AA", ecolor="#666666", capsize=3,
)
ax.set_yticks(list(positions), detail_summary.index)
ax.set(xlabel="Recorded closure time (hours)",
       title="Medians and middle-half ranges by problem detail")
ax.grid(axis="x", color="0.9")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The visual design changes the question a reader can answer from the same
closure-time records summarized in @sec-eda. Sorting the three details by
their medians and placing the dots on one horizontal scale makes their
central ordering easy to inspect. The quartile intervals show substantial
within-group variation and overlap, so the distance between median dots
cannot be read as separation between individual requests. The marks do
not encode group counts or the longest closure intervals; those quantities
remain in the exploratory tables and cumulative distributions. This is a
deliberate reduction of information for a focused comparison, and its
caption names the statistic represented by each mark. If delayed closures
were the communication goal, an upper-tail quantile or cumulative display
would be more appropriate. The figure also remains descriptive: a visual
gap between groups does not identify the effect of a problem-detail label
when reporting time, location, and administrative practices may differ.

## Common Mistakes {#sec-viz-common-mistakes}

Misleading figures can arise at several points between the source data and
the reader's conclusion. Selection can change which observations are
eligible; aggregation can suppress variation; visual encoding can make
small differences appear large; and a title can convert a descriptive
association into an unsupported causal claim. These are distinct failure
mechanisms, so a review confined to axis labels or color choice is
insufficient. Wainer cataloged recurring ways to obscure data, while later
work experimentally studied visual distortion and classified misleading
figures in published material [@tufte2001visual; @wainer1984how;
@pandey2015deceptive; @lo2022misinformed]. The operational review question
is what inference a reasonable viewer is likely to draw and whether the
selected records and displayed quantity justify it. This standard does not
depend on the maker's intent. A polished plot can still communicate the
wrong denominator, conceal a distribution, or suggest a relationship that
the study design cannot identify. @tbl-viz-mistakes summarizes recurring
choices, a deliberately poor example for each one, and a corresponding
diagnostic check. The examples use the illegal-parking extract or small
simulated data and are intentionally misleading; their captions identify
the defect rather than endorse the claim.

| Mistake and likely false inference | Bad-plot example | Check or repair | References |
|---|---|---|---|
| Records without usable coordinates are dropped; the plot appears to include all requests. | @fig-viz-mistake-selection | Report the excluded count and label the figure as geocoded records, or use a field that supports the full eligible set. | [@lo2022misinformed; @tufte2001visual] |
| A bar axis starts above zero; small differences appear large in length. | @fig-viz-baseline | Restore zero for a length encoding, or use aligned points when a restricted range is justified. | [@correll2020truncating] |
| Panels use different scales without a clear cue; similar heights appear comparable. | @fig-viz-mistake-facets | Use fixed scales for comparisons of level, or state prominently that each panel has its own scale. | [@tufte2001visual; @wainer1984how] |
| A mean or median appears alone; groups appear to have little internal variation. | @fig-viz-summary-loss | Add a distribution, observations, or a defined interval suited to the sample size. | [@weissgerber2015beyond; @correll2014error] |
| Bubble area exaggerates a value; larger circles look disproportionately larger. | @fig-viz-mistake-bubbles | Encode magnitude with aligned positions or lengths, or scale circle area rather than radius. | [@cleveland1984graphical] |
| A rainbow palette is used for an ordered measure; color bands suggest unsupported thresholds. | @fig-viz-mistake-rainbow | Choose an ordered, perceptually consistent palette. | [@crameri2020misuse; @harrower2003colorbrewer] |
| An area map shows request counts; darker areas appear to have greater illegal-parking risk. | @fig-viz-mistake-count-map | Examine a suitable denominator and retain the count map for context. | [@openshaw1984modifiable; @robinson1950ecological] |
| A title claims a cause or citywide trend; a one-week association appears to establish that claim. | @fig-viz-mistake-title | State the observation period and measured quantity; separate description from explanation. | [@heer2010crowdsourcing; @tufte2001visual] |

: Common visualization mistakes, their misleading examples, and checks for revision. {#tbl-viz-mistakes}

The first example drops requests without usable coordinates but gives the
remaining counts a title that implies full coverage. This selection can
change borough comparisons if missing locations are not distributed evenly.
The repair should either use all eligible borough records or state that the
figure summarizes geocoded requests and report how many records were
excluded.

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-mistake-selection
#| fig-cap: "A misleading title implies that all requests are counted, although the plot excludes records without usable coordinates."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of borough request counts based only on geocoded records, titled as if it includes every request."
#| fig-format: svg
geocoded_by_borough = (
    parking.dropna(subset=["latitude", "longitude"])
    .groupby("borough")
    .size()
    .reindex(borough_order, fill_value=0)
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.bar(geocoded_by_borough.index, geocoded_by_borough.values,
       color="#4477AA")
ax.set(title="All illegal-parking requests by borough",
       ylabel="Recorded requests")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=25)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The faceted example uses borough-specific vertical scales without
explaining that they differ. This makes the local peaks appear similar even
though the request levels are not. Fixed scales allow level comparisons; free
scales can help readers compare within-borough shape, but the caption and
axes must make that purpose clear.

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-mistake-facets
#| fig-cap: "A misleading faceted plot: each borough has its own vertical range, so similar panel heights do not indicate similar request levels."
#| fig-alt: "Five borough panels show weekday and weekend request rates with free vertical scales, making the peaks appear similar despite different levels."
#| fig-format: svg
(
    ggplot(hourly, aes("hour", "requests_per_day", color="day_type"))
    + geom_line(size=.8)
    + facet_wrap("borough", ncol=3, scales="free_y")
    + scale_color_manual(values={"Weekday": "#3366AA", "Weekend": "#CC6677"})
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=[0, 12, 23])
    + labs(x="Hour request was created", y="Requests per observed day",
           color="Day type", title="Similar hourly request levels by borough")
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(figure_size=(10, 6))
)
```

Baseline decisions should follow the visual quantity the reader is asked
to compare. A bar represents a numerical value through its length from a
common origin; when the origin is cut off, the apparent ratios between bar
lengths no longer represent ratios between values. A line or dot plot
primarily uses position, so a restricted range can help expose a small
change if the axis limits are conspicuous and the plot does not invite an
unwarranted comparison of physical lengths. Truncation can nevertheless
alter perceived effect size across chart types, even when a visual cue
signals the change [@correll2020truncating]. The paired figure holds the
three median closure times fixed and changes only the horizontal limits.
The left panel makes the differences occupy a larger fraction of the
available bar length; the right panel restores the zero baseline required
for a literal length comparison. Both panels omit the within-group spread
shown in @fig-viz-detail-intervals, which is a separate loss of information.

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-baseline
#| fig-cap: "Identical median closure times with a truncated baseline (left) and a zero baseline (right). The left bars exaggerate differences in length."
#| fig-alt: "Two horizontal bar charts show the same three median closure times. The left axis begins above zero, making differences appear larger."
#| fig-format: svg
medians = detail_summary["median"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8), sharey=True)
for ax in axes:
    ax.barh(medians.index, medians, color="#3366AA")
    ax.set_xlabel("Median closure time (hours)")
axes[0].set_xlim(medians.min() * .85, medians.max() * 1.08)
axes[0].set_title("Truncated baseline")
axes[1].set_xlim(0, medians.max() * 1.08)
axes[1].set_title("Zero baseline")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Summary statistics can conceal differences even when the axes and scales
are technically correct. In the following constructed example, both groups
have a mean of two units. Group A contains three zeroes and two fives,
whereas all five observations in group B equal two. The equal-height bars
correctly display the two means, but they cannot communicate the different
concentration and range of the observations. The point display retains the
five individual values in each group and makes that difference visible.
This example isolates information loss due to aggregation; it does not show
that individual points are always the appropriate marks. Thousands of
service requests would create severe overplotting, for which a histogram,
empirical cumulative distribution, density display, or selected quantiles
could better represent variation. The choice depends on whether the
question concerns center, spread, tail behavior, or individual cases, and
on how many observations can be displayed legibly
[@weissgerber2015beyond; @correll2014error].

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-summary-loss
#| fig-cap: "Two simulated groups have the same mean but different observed distributions."
#| fig-alt: "Equal-height mean bars conceal that group A has values at zero and five while every value in group B is two."
#| fig-format: svg
simulated = {"A": np.array([0, 0, 0, 5, 5]),
             "B": np.array([2, 2, 2, 2, 2])}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.7))
axes[0].bar(list(simulated), [values.mean() for values in simulated.values()],
            color="#3366AA")
axes[0].set(title="Means only", ylabel="Observed value", ylim=(0, 6))
for position, (name, values) in enumerate(simulated.items()):
    offsets = np.linspace(-.13, .13, len(values))
    axes[1].scatter(position + offsets, values, color="#3366AA", s=35)
axes[1].set(xticks=[0, 1], xticklabels=list(simulated),
            title="Individual values", ylabel="Observed value", ylim=(0, 6))
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The next plot uses circle radius, rather than circle area, to encode median
closure time. Because the area of a circle grows with the square of its
radius, this choice exaggerates differences between the three problem
details. A position or length encoding supports more reliable comparisons.

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-mistake-bubbles
#| fig-cap: "A misleading bubble plot: circle radius is proportional to median closure time, so circle area exaggerates the differences."
#| fig-alt: "Three circles represent median closure times, with radii proportional to the values and areas therefore growing quadratically."
#| fig-format: svg
bubble_values = detail_summary["median"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
x_positions = np.arange(len(bubble_values))
ax.scatter(x_positions, np.zeros(len(bubble_values)),
           s=(bubble_values.to_numpy() * 30) ** 2,
           color="#4477AA", alpha=.65)
ax.set(xticks=x_positions, xticklabels=bubble_values.index,
       yticks=[], title="Median closure time shown by bubble radius")
for spine in ["left", "right", "top"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Color and annotation should be evaluated by the comparisons they enable.
Distinct hues can identify unordered categories; progressively ordered
lightness can represent increasing magnitude; and a diverging scale is
appropriate when a defined reference, such as zero change, separates two
directions. An uneven gradient can create apparent thresholds where the
data are continuous, while a distinction conveyed only by red and green
can be inaccessible to some readers [@crameri2020misuse;
@harrower2003colorbrewer]. Decoration is not categorically harmful:
experiments with embellished figures complicate a blanket prohibition
[@bateman2010useful]. The appropriate test is whether an element helps
readers locate or compare evidence without implying an unsupported result.
Every plot should also be reviewed as a claim. Its title should match the
measured quantity; its axes and legend should state units; and its caption
should identify the source, observation period, aggregation, and exclusions.
When a figure is revised, the analyst should inspect the source records
again to confirm that the repaired display still represents the intended
population and denominator.

The final example gives one week of request counts a title that claims a
citywide trend. The bars describe recorded requests in this extract; they
do not establish a long-term increase in illegal parking across New York
City. The repaired title and caption should name the observation period
and avoid extending the conclusion beyond the available records.

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-mistake-title
#| fig-cap: "A misleading title turns one week of recorded request counts into an unsupported citywide trend claim."
#| fig-alt: "Daily illegal-parking request counts from September 6 through September 12, 2026, shown under a title claiming a citywide increase."
#| fig-format: svg
daily_counts = parking.groupby(parking["created_at"].dt.normalize()).size()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.8))
ax.bar(daily_counts.index, daily_counts.values, color="#4477AA")
ax.set(title="Illegal parking is increasing across New York City",
       xlabel="Date in the one-week extract", ylabel="Recorded requests")
fig.autofmt_xdate()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Maps

Spatial graphics add a choice of geographic unit to the visual design.
The 311 extract supplies recorded coordinates for most requests, while
NYC Open Data supplies polygons for 221 ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs)
[@nycopendata2026zip]. A point map retains the approximate location of an
individual request and can expose concentration or gaps at a fine scale,
subject to overlapping marks and geocoding quality. A choropleth instead
assigns one aggregate value to an entire polygon, which supports area
comparison but removes within-area variation. The maps answer different
questions even when they use the same request archive. The choice between
them should follow the intended comparison: where reports were recorded,
how many matched an area, or how an area summary varies across the city.
Population estimates from @sec-zcta-context-merge can provide one possible
denominator, but the resulting rate still measures requests per resident
over the stated period. The map's color and legend must identify that
quantity rather than imply verified illegal-parking prevalence.

The geometry construction makes the coordinate reference system explicit.
The request coordinates are recorded as longitude and latitude, so the
point table is created with the geographic system EPSG:4326. The ZCTA
boundaries are read from a compact local file derived from the official NYC
source; its [provenance note](data/nyc_zcta_boundaries.md) records the
derivation and boundary simplification. GeoPandas uses coordinate reference
system metadata to transform geometries, but a declared system does not
verify that every source coordinate is accurate. The static figures use
New York State Plane coordinates (EPSG:2263) so that the city is displayed
in a suitable projected system. Projection is especially important for
distance or area calculations because longitude and latitude are angular
coordinates, and a degree of longitude does not represent a constant
ground distance. A projection changes the representation of a recorded
location; it cannot repair a wrong address, an approximate geocode, or a
missing coordinate [@geopandas2026projections].

```{python}
zcta_polygons = gpd.read_file(Path("data") / "nyc_zcta_boundaries.geojson")
zcta_context = load_zcta_context()
with_coordinates = parking.dropna(subset=["latitude", "longitude"]).copy()
request_points = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    with_coordinates,
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(
        with_coordinates["longitude"], with_coordinates["latitude"]
    ),
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
pd.Series({
    "requests in scope": len(parking),
    "requests with coordinates": len(request_points),
    "ZCTA polygons": len(zcta_polygons),
}).to_frame("count")
```

A point map with many observations needs a display rule that accounts for
overlap. Several requests can share a geocoded address, and opaque markers
would cover earlier marks at the same or nearby positions. The following
figure therefore uses a reproducible random sample of 2,000 geocoded
requests and draws small, transparent points over ZCTA outlines. Sampling
reduces the number of overlapping marks while preserving, in expectation,
the distribution of locations among geocoded records. It also makes the
plot unsuitable for reading exact counts at a location: the absence of a
sampled point does not imply the absence of requests. Transparency helps
show accumulation, but apparent density still depends on point size,
opacity, and map scale. The polygon outlines provide orientation rather
than an area-level measurement. A density surface would introduce further
choices, especially a smoothing bandwidth and treatment of boundaries;
those choices would need to be reported before the surface could support a
quantitative comparison.

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-request-points
#| fig-cap: "A reproducible sample of 2,000 geocoded illegal-parking requests over NYC ZCTA boundaries, September 6–12, 2026."
#| fig-alt: "Small transparent points from a 2,000-request sample appear over outlines of New York City ZIP Code Tabulation Areas."
#| fig-format: svg
sample_points = request_points.sample(n=2000, random_state=2026)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))
zcta_polygons.to_crs("EPSG:2263").boundary.plot(
    ax=ax, color="#999999", linewidth=.3
)
sample_points.to_crs("EPSG:2263").plot(
    ax=ax, color="#225588", markersize=3, alpha=.3
)
ax.set_axis_off()
ax.set_title("Recorded request locations and ZCTA boundaries")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

An area map requires an assignment rule that maps each request to a named
polygon or reports why it remains unassigned. @sec-zcta-context-merge
used equality of the provider's five-digit postal ZIP label and a Census
ZCTA code; it also explained why equal labels do not imply identical
geographies [@census2023zip]. Coordinates permit an alternative
point-in-polygon assignment. That operation answers a different question,
because it uses the recorded point rather than the provider's postal label.
It requires valid coordinates, a selected polygon file, and a spatial
predicate. Under `within`, a point exactly on a boundary does not belong
to either adjoining polygon, while overlaps can assign one request to
several polygons. An imprecise geocode or simplified boundary can also
change a near-edge match. Before shading a map, the analyst should count
one-to-one, unmatched, and multiple assignments and decide which rule
corresponds to the geographic target. The diagnostic below makes those
outcomes visible for the supplied ZCTA polygons [@nycopendata2026zip].

```{python}
point_zcta = gpd.sjoin(
    request_points[["request_id", "incident_zip", "geometry"]],
    zcta_polygons[["zcta", "geometry"]],
    how="left", predicate="within",
)
match_count = point_zcta.groupby(level=0)["zcta"].count()
pd.Series({
    "one polygon": match_count.eq(1).sum(),
    "no polygon": match_count.eq(0).sum(),
    "more than one polygon": match_count.gt(1).sum(),
}).to_frame("geocoded requests")
```

The spatial diagnostic shows that 21 geocoded requests have no polygon
match and 28 have more than one match in the compact boundary file. These
counts establish that the join cannot be substituted silently for the
provider's ZIP field. A boundary point may fail the `within` predicate;
overlapping polygons may produce multiple rows for one request; and
boundary simplification can change a near-edge result. Each mechanism
requires a different response. For a precise point-to-area study, the
analyst should inspect the ambiguous records against the original
boundaries, state a tie-breaking rule if one is justified, and report the
remaining exclusions. The maps below instead retain the ZIP-label match
introduced in @sec-zcta-context-merge, which keeps their area summaries
comparable to the earlier data-preparation example. The point-in-polygon
results remain a diagnostic of geographic disagreement rather than an
unexamined source of replacement labels.

The paired choropleths separate the effect of a numerator from the effect
of a denominator. For ZCTA $z$, let $N_z$ be the number of selected requests
whose valid five-digit provider ZIP label matches its code, and let $P_z$
be its 2020–2024 American Community Survey population estimate. The first
map shows $N_z$; the second shows $10{,}000N_z/P_z$ when $P_z>0$. Its unit
is requests per 10,000 estimated residents during the selected week.
The formula does not measure the probability that a resident experiences
illegal parking, because the numerator consists of requests rather than
verified events and the population is not the number of parking
opportunities. It also combines 2026 requests with an earlier population
estimate. Twenty-seven ZCTAs have a zero population estimate; their rates
are undefined and appear in gray rather than as zero. A polygon with no
matched ZIP-label requests can still contain geocoded requests assigned
another label. Both maps use ordered color, but separate legends identify
their different quantities and units [@harrower2003colorbrewer;
@crameri2020misuse].

```{python}
valid_zip = parking["incident_zip"].str.fullmatch(r"\d{5}", na=False)
area_counts = (
    parking.loc[valid_zip]
    .groupby("incident_zip")
    .size()
    .rename("requests")
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns={"incident_zip": "zcta"})
)
area_map = (
    zcta_polygons
    .merge(zcta_context[["zcta", "population"]],
           on="zcta", validate="one_to_one")
    .merge(area_counts, on="zcta", how="left", validate="one_to_one")
)
area_map["requests"] = area_map["requests"].fillna(0).astype(int)
area_map["requests_per_10k"] = np.where(
    area_map["population"].gt(0),
    area_map["requests"] / area_map["population"] * 10_000,
    np.nan,
)
```

The next two plots illustrate the map-specific mistakes in
@tbl-viz-mistakes. The first pairs a continuous rate with a rainbow palette,
which can suggest abrupt boundaries that are not present in the data. The
second presents counts as risk even though ZCTAs differ in population and
other exposure. The count map can describe service workload, but it does
not by itself identify where illegal parking is more likely.

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-mistake-rainbow
#| fig-cap: "A misleading choropleth: the rainbow palette introduces strong hue boundaries into a continuous request rate."
#| fig-alt: "New York City ZCTA polygons colored by requests per 10,000 residents with a rainbow gradient."
#| fig-format: svg
projected_map = area_map.to_crs("EPSG:2263")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
projected_map.plot(column="requests_per_10k", cmap="rainbow", legend=True,
                   ax=ax, missing_kwds={"color": "#bdbdbd"})
ax.set_title("Requests per 10,000 residents (rainbow scale)")
ax.set_axis_off()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-mistake-count-map
#| fig-cap: "A misleading choropleth: raw request counts are titled as illegal-parking risk, although areas differ in population and exposure."
#| fig-alt: "New York City ZCTA polygons show raw illegal-parking request counts under a title claiming to show risk."
#| fig-format: svg
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
projected_map.plot(column="requests", cmap="OrRd", legend=True, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Illegal-parking risk by ZCTA")
ax.set_axis_off()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-zcta-maps
#| fig-cap: "Illegal-parking request counts (left) and requests per 10,000 estimated residents (right) by matched NYC ZCTA label, September 6–12, 2026. Gray areas have undefined rates because their population estimate is zero."
#| fig-alt: "Two New York City ZCTA choropleths display request counts and population-adjusted request rates with separate legends."
#| fig-format: svg
projected_map = area_map.to_crs("EPSG:2263")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6))
for ax, variable, title in [
    (axes[0], "requests", "Recorded requests"),
    (axes[1], "requests_per_10k", "Requests per 10,000 residents"),
]:
    projected_map.plot(
        column=variable, ax=ax, cmap="viridis", legend=True,
        legend_kwds={"shrink": .6}, edgecolor="white", linewidth=.15,
        missing_kwds={"color": "#dddddd", "label": "Rate unavailable"},
    )
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_axis_off()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Differences between the count and rate maps require substantive
interpretation before they are treated as evidence of geographic risk.
Residential population need not be proportional to the number of drivers,
visitors, curb spaces, or people likely to report a problem. A commercial
area with few residents can therefore have a high per-resident request rate
without having an unusually high number of requests. Map color also
depends on the chosen boundaries: combining ZCTAs into boroughs can conceal
local variation, while a different grouping of neighborhoods can change
the apparent association between location and requests
[@openshaw1984modifiable; @armstrong2014visualizing]. Even a stable
area-level pattern does not establish the behavior or exposure of
individual residents [@robinson1950ecological]. A defensible map should
therefore state the numerator, denominator, time period, assignment rule,
and treatment of unmatched records. The analyst should also ask whether
the geographic arrangement answers a question that a sorted table or dot
plot could not answer as clearly.

## Interactive Maps

An interactive figure is useful when a reader has a specific task that a
static display cannot perform as conveniently. A reader may need to find a
ZCTA, inspect its exact value, or move between a citywide view and a local
street context. Interaction does not correct a weak denominator, uncertain
geocode, or unsupported interpretation; those analytical decisions are
fixed before a tooltip or zoom control is added. GeoPandas `.explore()`
uses Folium and Leaflet to generate the interactive map below from the
same ZCTA summaries as the static choropleths. Its polygon color represents
the per-resident request rate, while its tooltip reports the ZCTA code,
request count, population estimate, and calculated rate. Showing the
numerator and denominator next to the rate helps readers diagnose an
unusually high value. The static companion remains necessary for readers
who cannot interact with the page and for a stable comparison of the full
city at one scale. The example uses CARTO's Positron basemap when a
basemap key is available and falls back to OpenStreetMap otherwise. The
CARTO key is supplied through the `CARTO_BASEMAP_API_KEY` environment
variable or a local `cartoBaseAPIKey.txt` file in the project root. CARTO
requires a key for these tile services and requires visible attribution
[@geopandas2026interactive; @carto2026basemaps].
The key appears in browser tile requests and can be inspected in the
generated page. Restrict it to the intended site or local preview, keep
the key file out of version control, and do not publish a generated page
that contains an unrestricted key [@carto2026basemaps].

```{python}
#| label: fig-viz-interactive-map
#| fig-cap: "Interactive ZCTA map of recorded requests per 10,000 estimated residents. Hover to inspect the count and denominator."
#| fig-alt: "Interactive New York City ZCTA map with a legend and tooltips for area code, request count, population estimate, and request rate."
import os
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import quote

carto_key = os.environ.get("CARTO_BASEMAP_API_KEY")
if carto_key is None and Path("cartoBaseAPIKey.txt").exists():
    carto_key = Path("cartoBaseAPIKey.txt").read_text().strip()

tile_options = {"tiles": "OpenStreetMap"}
if carto_key:
    tile_options = {
        "tiles": (
            "https://basemaps.cartocdn.com/rastertiles/light_all/"
            f"{{z}}/{{x}}/{{y}}.png?key={quote(carto_key, safe='')}"
        ),
        "attr": "© OpenStreetMap contributors, © CARTO",
    }

interactive_map = area_map.loc[area_map["population"].gt(0)].explore(
    column="requests_per_10k",
    cmap="viridis",
    tooltip=["zcta", "requests", "population", "requests_per_10k"],
    legend=True,
    **tile_options,
)
interactive_map
```

Interactive design requires a hierarchy between what is visible at first
glance and what is available on request. In this example, color provides
an overview of the rate, and the tooltip reveals exact values needed to
understand its construction. Adding every source field to the tooltip
would shift work to the reader without improving the comparison. The map
also omits the 27 areas with zero estimated population because their
per-resident rates are undefined; the static map marks them in gray. This
difference in eligibility should be stated when the two displays are
presented together. Online tile layers can fail to load, and hover
interaction can be difficult to use with a keyboard or on a touch device.
A static counterpart, concise text description, and accessible table of
key values preserve the principal result when interaction is unavailable.
The evaluation questions remain the same as for static figures: which
records are represented, which quantity is encoded, and which comparison
does the display allow a reader to make?

Google Maps can provide an alternative basemap for the same ZCTA choropleth.
The Maps JavaScript API data layer accepts GeoJSON polygons and supports
feature-based styling and click events. The example below transfers the
already prepared `area_map` to GeoJSON, styles ZCTAs by the same
requests-per-resident measure, and opens a detail window when a reader
selects a polygon [@google2026datalayer]. It uses quantile breaks calculated
from the displayed areas, so the legend reports the class boundaries used
by this dataset; its colors therefore do not match the continuous Folium
scale one for one. The Folium version remains the default and uses
OpenStreetMap if a CARTO key is unavailable.

The Google version runs only when an API key is supplied through the
`GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` environment variable. The key must be enabled for the
Maps JavaScript API, restricted to that API and to the site or local server
that will display the map, and associated with billing. The generated HTML
contains the browser key and should stay local; do not commit it or publish
it with the book [@google2026maps; @google2026billing].

```{python}
#| eval: false
import json
import os
from html import escape
from pathlib import Path

google_geojson = json.loads(
    area_map.to_crs("EPSG:4326").to_json(drop_id=True)
)
google_geojson_json = json.dumps(
    google_geojson, separators=(",", ":"), allow_nan=False
).replace("</", "<\\/")
rate_breaks = np.unique(
    area_map["requests_per_10k"].dropna().quantile([0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8])
).tolist()
colors = ["#ffffcc", "#a1dab4", "#41b6c4", "#2c7fb8", "#253494"]
colors = colors[:len(rate_breaks) + 1]
rate_labels = [
    f"≤ {rate_breaks[0]:.2f}",
    *[
        f"{lower:.2f}–{upper:.2f}"
        for lower, upper in zip(rate_breaks[:-1], rate_breaks[1:])
    ],
    f"> {rate_breaks[-1]:.2f}",
]
api_key = escape(os.environ["GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY"], quote=True)
google_map_html = f"""<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Illegal-parking requests by ZCTA</title>
  <style>
    #map {{ height: 90vh; width: 100%; }}
    #legend {{ background: white; padding: 10px; margin: 10px;
              font: 14px sans-serif; }}
    .swatch {{ display: inline-block; width: 12px; height: 12px;
               margin-right: 6px; }}
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <div id="map" role="application"
       aria-label="Interactive map of NYC ZCTA request rates"></div>
  <script>
    const zctaData = {google_geojson_json};
    const rateBreaks = {json.dumps(rate_breaks)};
    const colors = {json.dumps(colors)};
    const rateLabels = {json.dumps(rate_labels)};

    async function initMap() {{
      const {{ Map, InfoWindow }} = await google.maps.importLibrary("maps");
      const map = new Map(document.getElementById("map"), {{
        center: {{ lat: 40.7128, lng: -74.0060 }},
        zoom: 10,
        mapTypeId: "roadmap",
      }});
      const infoWindow = new InfoWindow();
      map.data.addGeoJson(zctaData);
      map.data.setStyle((feature) => {{
        const rate = feature.getProperty("requests_per_10k");
        const classIndex = rate == null
          ? -1
          : rateBreaks.findIndex((upper) => Number(rate) <= upper);
        const fillColor = classIndex < 0
          ? (rate == null ? "#bdbdbd" : colors[colors.length - 1])
          : colors[classIndex];
        return {{
          fillColor: fillColor,
          fillOpacity: 0.7,
          strokeColor: "#ffffff",
          strokeWeight: 1,
        }};
      }});
      map.data.addListener("click", (event) => {{
        const feature = event.feature;
        const rate = feature.getProperty("requests_per_10k");
        const rateText = rate == null
          ? "Undefined: zero estimated population"
          : `${{Number(rate).toFixed(2)}} requests per 10,000 residents`;
        const content = document.createElement("div");
        content.textContent =
          `ZCTA ${{feature.getProperty("zcta")}} | ` +
          `${{feature.getProperty("requests")}} requests | ` +
          `${{feature.getProperty("population")}} residents | ${{rateText}}`;
        infoWindow.setContent(content);
        infoWindow.setPosition(event.latLng);
        infoWindow.open({{ map }});
      }});

      const legend = document.createElement("div");
      legend.id = "legend";
      legend.innerHTML = rateLabels.map((label, index) =>
        `<div><span class="swatch" style="background:${{colors[index]}}"></span>${{label}}</div>`
      ).join("") +
        '<div><span class="swatch" style="background:#bdbdbd"></span>Rate undefined</div>';
      map.controls[google.maps.ControlPosition.RIGHT_BOTTOM].push(legend);
    }}

    window.initMap = initMap;
  </script>
  <script async
    src="https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/js?key={api_key}&callback=initMap&v=weekly">
  </script>
</body>
</html>
"""
Path("parking_requests_google_zcta.html").write_text(
    google_map_html, encoding="utf-8"
)
print("Wrote parking_requests_google_zcta.html")

```

The choice between interactive tools should follow the geographic question
and the intended reader action. The GeoPandas–Folium–Leaflet route uses
the local ZCTA geometries and runs in the book environment; it supports
inspection of the area summaries already constructed. A Google map may be
appropriate when the question requires a familiar street basemap or a
particular Google service, but the optional example requires key management
and produces a separate HTML page. Neither tool decides whether a point
should be assigned to an area, which distance measure is substantively
relevant, or whether a route is a valid proxy for travel time. For example,
straight-line distance from a complaint location to a police precinct is
different from network distance and does not include dispatch procedures.
A project should therefore define the reader's task, geographic operation,
and units before selecting the interface. It should also account for
accessibility, reproducibility, and any information sent to an external
map service.

## Animate Change

Animation extends a static display by changing one part of the figure across
frames. Matplotlib's `FuncAnimation` repeatedly calls an update function,
which changes the marks or data shown for the current frame. A useful
animation keeps scales and spatial extents fixed, labels the frame in plain
language, and changes only what the question requires. Animation can expose
timing or accumulation that is difficult to see in a static figure, but
rapid movement can also make comparisons harder. A static summary should
remain available for readers who need to compare values across the full
period. The examples use the week of illegal-parking requests to animate a
borough count and the spatial distribution of recorded locations
[@matplotlib2026funcanimation].

The first animation shows cumulative request counts by borough at the end
of each day. Each frame adds a day of observations, so the bar lengths show
how the total grows over the week. A fixed horizontal scale keeps lengths
comparable from frame to frame. The animation describes request volume in
this extract; it does not measure illegal-parking prevalence or borough
performance.

```{python}
import base64
import tempfile

from IPython.display import HTML
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

def display_gif(animation, *, alt_text, caption):
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".gif") as gif_file:
        animation.save(gif_file.name, writer="pillow", fps=1, dpi=90)
        encoded_gif = base64.b64encode(
            Path(gif_file.name).read_bytes()
        ).decode("ascii")
        return HTML(
            f'<figure><img src="data:image/gif;base64,{encoded_gif}" '
            f'alt="{alt_text}"><figcaption>{caption}</figcaption></figure>'
        )

daily_borough_counts = (
    parking.assign(date=parking["created_at"].dt.normalize())
    .groupby(["date", "borough"])
    .size()
    .unstack(fill_value=0)
    .reindex(
        index=pd.date_range(
            parking["created_at"].min().normalize(),
            parking["created_at"].max().normalize(),
            freq="D",
        ),
        columns=borough_order,
        fill_value=0,
    )
    .sort_index()
    .cumsum()
)
```

The update function redraws the horizontal bars for the date associated with
each frame. The animation is saved as a GIF with Matplotlib's Pillow writer;
the file is created temporarily during rendering, so the figure does not
add a generated binary to the repository. The `FuncAnimation` object remains
assigned to `count_animation` while the GIF is written, which prevents it
from being discarded before all frames are rendered.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
count_limit = daily_borough_counts.to_numpy().max() * 1.1

def update_count(frame):
    ax.clear()
    counts = daily_borough_counts.iloc[frame]
    ax.barh(counts.index, counts.values, color="#3366AA")
    ax.set_xlim(0, count_limit)
    ax.set_xlabel("Cumulative requests")
    ax.set_title(
        f"Requests through {daily_borough_counts.index[frame]:%b %d, %Y}"
    )
    ax.invert_yaxis()

count_animation = FuncAnimation(
    fig, update_count, frames=range(len(daily_borough_counts)),
    interval=700, repeat=False,
)
count_gif = display_gif(
    count_animation,
    alt_text="An animated horizontal bar chart shows cumulative request counts increasing across five New York City boroughs over seven days.",
    caption="Cumulative number of illegal-parking requests recorded in each borough by date, September 6–12, 2026.",
)
plt.close(fig)
count_gif
```

The map animation changes the points while retaining the same ZCTA outlines
and projected view in every frame. Each frame displays requests created on
one calendar day, using the coordinates supplied with the request data.
The same geocoding limitations described for the static point map apply:
overlapping locations can obscure one another, and an approximate point
does not establish the exact location of an event. The display shows where
requests were recorded, not how vehicles moved. It uses locally stored
boundaries and does not depend on a live basemap, which makes the animation
reproducible when the book is built.

```{python}
map_points = request_points.to_crs("EPSG:2263")
map_boundaries = zcta_polygons.to_crs("EPSG:2263")
frame_dates = pd.date_range(
    parking["created_at"].min().normalize(),
    parking["created_at"].max().normalize(),
    freq="D",
)
min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y = map_boundaries.total_bounds
x_margin = (max_x - min_x) * 0.03
y_margin = (max_y - min_y) * 0.03

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
map_boundaries.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="#999999", linewidth=0.3)
points = ax.scatter([], [], color="#225588", s=5, alpha=0.45)
frame_title = ax.set_title("")
ax.set_xlim(min_x - x_margin, max_x + x_margin)
ax.set_ylim(min_y - y_margin, max_y + y_margin)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_axis_off()

def update_map(frame):
    date = frame_dates[frame]
    current = map_points.loc[
        map_points["created_at"].dt.normalize().eq(date)
    ]
    coordinates = np.column_stack((current.geometry.x, current.geometry.y))
    points.set_offsets(coordinates)
    frame_title.set_text(
        f"Recorded requests on {date:%b %d, %Y} (n = {len(current):,})"
    )
    return points, frame_title

map_animation = FuncAnimation(
    fig, update_map, frames=range(len(frame_dates)),
    interval=700, repeat=False,
)
map_gif = display_gif(
    map_animation,
    alt_text="An animated map shows daily points for geocoded illegal-parking requests over fixed outlines of New York City ZCTAs.",
    caption="Geocoded illegal-parking request locations by day against NYC ZCTA boundaries, September 6–12, 2026.",
)
plt.close(fig)
map_gif
```

The two animations make different comparisons: the bars emphasize
accumulation, while the map shows the daily distribution of recorded
locations. Neither should be read as evidence of a stable pattern from one
week. The animation can direct attention to dates or places for follow-up;
the static hourly, daily, and area summaries elsewhere in this chapter
provide more reliable comparisons across groups. Students should state the
frame unit, whether values accumulate or reset, the fixed scales, and the
data excluded from each animation.

The same visual discipline applies when the course moves from description
to modeling. A predicted-versus-observed plot can show where a model
systematically overpredicts or underpredicts an outcome; a residual plot
can reveal structure that an average error measure conceals. Neither plot
is interpretable until the target, prediction unit, eligible observations,
and evaluation data are defined. A plot of training residuals, for
example, answers a different question from one based on held-out
predictions. @sec-modeling develops that framework. The present chapter
establishes the complementary visual procedure: preserve units, expose
variation relevant to the question, label transformations and exclusions,
and check whether the displayed evidence supports the claim in the title
and interpretation [@munzner2014visualization; @yu2024veridical]. These
requirements make a figure useful across exploration, communication, and
model diagnosis. They also give students a way to revise a first attempt:
identify the inference the reader is invited to make, then inspect each
data and design decision that supports it.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

The exercises move from a specified comparison to a self-directed project
question. Submit source code, rendered figures, captions, and brief written
interpretations. For each figure, identify the row unit, eligible records,
variables, visual mappings, source, observation period, and a limit on the
claim. For a new NYC Open Data source, record its dataset identifier, access
date, relevant data-dictionary definitions, and any filtering or aggregation.
An attractive plot alone does not satisfy these requirements.

::: {#exr-viz-grammar}
Use the results of @exr-eda-time to visualize how the proportion of requests
taking at least two hours to close varies across the four six-hour creation
intervals and problem details. Use the same threshold and eligible records;
focus on translating the EDA comparison into a figure rather than rebuilding
its contingency tables.

a. Use the three most frequent problem details identified in the EDA
   exercise. Construct one plot with color and one with facets. Explain which
   comparison becomes easier in each, and show the number of eligible
   requests behind the proportions.
b. Build a `facet_grid()` with problem detail in rows and borough in columns.
   Explain what fixed vertical scales allow readers to compare. Then use free
   vertical scales and explain how the interpretation changes.
c. State the denominator for each plotted proportion and how requests with
   missing closure time are handled. Explain one way unequal group sizes
   affect interpretation and identify a limitation that remains.
:::

::: {#exr-viz-repair}
Create and repair two misleading plots from the illegal-parking data. Use
two *different* mistakes from the table in @sec-viz-common-mistakes; at least
one must concern data selection, aggregation, or interpretation rather than
only styling.

a. For each pair, show the same underlying records and explain the inference
   the flawed version invites.
b. Revise the mapping, scale, summary, label, or caption as needed. State
   which information the repair reveals and which limitation it cannot fix.
c. Cite one of the chapter's empirical or methodological references that
   supports each revision. Explain how its finding applies to your example.
:::

::: {#exr-viz-space}
Investigate the geographic pattern of illegal-parking requests using both
the supplied point coordinates and the ZCTA boundary file.

a. Make a point map with a defensible display rule for overlap. Report the
   number of requests without coordinates and explain what a point means.
b. Compare the provider's five-digit ZIP-label match with a point-in-polygon
   spatial join. Report unmatched and multiply matched points before choosing
   an area-assignment rule.
c. Map one count and one normalized quantity. Define the denominator and
   explain why neither map alone measures the risk of illegal parking. Add
   an interactive version only if it helps a specified reader task.
:::

::: {#exr-viz-project}
Prepare a small visualization proposal for a midterm project. Select a
dataset beyond the distributed 311 extract, such as NYC Open Data's Motor
Vehicle Collisions or Parks Inspection Program records
[@nycopendata2026motor; @nycopendata2026parks].

a. State one question the data can address and one tempting question it
   cannot address without further information. Inspect the data dictionary
   before choosing a figure.
b. Make an exploratory graphic and revise it for an identified audience.
   Choose the chart form and tool yourself, and justify their visual
   mappings, aggregation, and any interaction.
c. Write a caption and alternative text. Record one analytical decision
   that changed after inspecting the first plot, and explain how you checked
   that decision against the source data.
:::

::: {#exr-viz-model}
After @sec-modeling, use held-out predictions from a model with a continuous
outcome to make a predicted-versus-observed plot and a residual plot. Define
the target, prediction unit, and held-out observations. Identify one pattern
that an average performance measure conceals, and explain what the plots
cannot establish about future observations.
:::
